doc.title: Tom Lellis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, July 31, 2007

title: Recording with the Metropole Orchestra
summary: He describes how Mark Murphy's tip led to a live recording with the Metropole Orchestra under John Clayton, working with arrangers Abene, Mendoza and Owen, and the tight rehearsal schedule.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: I see. Well if you could get in a time machine, is there a couple of moments — well not necessarily just jazz history — but maybe where would you like to go back to, to be a fly on the wall?
Yeah you know I guess I don’t think in terms like that. I think that hopefully one views their career as an ascent, you know, so for me going back, you mean historically?
I just mean like is there a record date or something that you’d like to have watched or something like that?

Well maybe Sinatra and Nelson Riddle or something like that era where there was a great arranger and a full orchestra and I could just not worry about anything but singing the song. You know, maybe that era, right.
Yeah. That must have been a heck of a feeling when you did that with the Metropole Orchestra. Did you do that live?

We did it live. Yeah. And John Clayton conducted. So it was the thrill of my life. It came out of the blue. Mark Murphy had told me to send my material to the Netherlands. And then I did, I sent the material and I got an email maybe eight months, nine months later, maybe a year. And the producer said that he just kept listening to my record. He just kept

playing it and he goes back to it. And he said, “I can’t promise you anything but I’m keeping you in mind.” And then I did a performance at the IAJE in New York in 1998 with Joe Locke and Tony Marino, who was just on the gig last night, and Jamey Haddad. And he was there and we signed a contract to do it the next day, for a year and a month later. I had to wait 13 months to do it, and it was the longest period. That was such a thrill. I had to keep my welled up tears down in the middle of a couple of those takes just ‘cause I was just — I did, out of the studio I did shed a few tears just of happiness. It was, my wife was there, it was a totally elating time, it was a thrill.
How much input did you have with your arrangers?

I spoke to Mike Abene and Vince Mendoza and Chuck Owen. But I didn’t speak to the Dutch arranger that arranged two tunes on that, and I was sorry, and I think the producer was kind of sorry. I think he didn’t want me to actually communicate with them too much. He wanted, you know, some individuality there and that we’d all come together. But I spoke and talked at length with three of the arrangers out of the four.
You gave them your keys and here’s my idea of —

Well conceptually, yeah. And then I know Mike Abene wrote in some extensions in the tunes and you’d get to the rehearsal and you’d find out then, the first day, what these charts sound like. You never hear them. So I got there on a Monday, I heard them rehearsing the charts Monday, we started rehearsing on Tuesday, and we were supposed to finish rehearsing on Wednesday and then record Thursday and Friday. No I’m sorry, we were supposed to rehearse one day and then begin recording on the second day. And we didn’t get through the rehearsals. The charts were tough and very involved. So we started recording late on Wednesday and we had Wednesday and Thursday and then we did fixes, the orchestra fixes and I had a couple on Friday and we were out of there. What a thrill though. It was just a great thrill. It’s something I never — you know it was a dream come true because there’s that Nelson Riddle Orchestra thing, and it was a total dream before that. And I’ll never forget that.
Kind of interesting that it happened across the pond as they say.
